maps.title: Ancient Israel
maps.subtitle: The Old Testament land, from Dan to Beersheba
maps.intro: Israel in the days of the kings and prophets, David's Jerusalem, Elijah's Mount Carmel, and the two kingdoms the land split into.

places.name: Jericho
places.note: the first city taken in Canaan

places.name: Megiddo
places.note: fortress city on the great road

places.name: Mount Carmel
places.note: Elijah vs. the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18)

places.name: Mount Nebo
places.note: where Moses saw the Promised Land

places.name: En Gedi
places.note: the oasis where David hid from Saul

facts: “From Dan to Beersheba” is how the Bible itself says “the whole land” (Judges 20:1), find both on the map and you have its length: about 150 miles, the distance of a long car day.
After Solomon, the land split in two: Israel in the north with its capital at Samaria, and Judah in the south with Jerusalem (1 Kings 12). Most prophet stories happen in one kingdom or the other.
The Jordan River connects the Sea of Galilee to the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea), the lowest place on the face of the earth, so salty nothing lives in it.

maps.title: Israel in Jesus' Time
maps.subtitle: Galilee, Samaria and Judea in the New Testament
maps.keyword: map of israel in jesus time
maps.intro: The same land, about a thousand years later, now under Rome, divided into the regions the Gospels name on nearly every page.

places.name: Bethsaida
places.note: hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip

places.name: Caesarea
places.note: Roman capital of the province; Peter and Cornelius

places.name: Sychar
places.note: the Samaritan woman at the well (John 4)

places.name: Emmaus
places.note: the road where the risen Jesus walked

facts: Almost every Gospel story happens in one of three regions: Galilee in the north (most of the ministry), Judea in the south (Bethlehem, Jerusalem, the cross), and Samaria between them, the region most travelers went around and Jesus walked through (John 4).

The Sea of Galilee is really a lake about 13 miles long, small enough that you can see across it, big enough for the storms the fishermen feared. Capernaum, Bethsaida and Tiberias all sit on its shore.

Nazareth to Jerusalem, the trip Mary and Joseph made, is about 90 miles on foot, four or five days of walking. Find both cities and trace the road down the Jordan valley through Jericho, the route most Galileans took.

maps.title: The Exodus
maps.subtitle: Out of Egypt, through the Red Sea, to Mount Sinai
maps.intro: The route from Pharaoh's Egypt to the edge of the Promised Land, the traditional path, with the places the story names along the way.
maps.disclaimer: The Bible names the stops; it does not give coordinates. This map follows the traditional southern route that pilgrims have used for over 1,500 years, Mount Sinai at Jebel Musa, the crossing near the Gulf of Suez. Scholars debate several of these sites, and the map marks the traditional ones with an asterisk.

places.name: Rameses
places.note: the store-city where Israel was enslaved; the journey starts here

places.name: Rephidim
places.note: water from the rock; battle with Amalek

places.name: Kadesh-barnea
places.note: the twelve spies; 38 years of waiting

places.name: Ezion-geber
places.note: port at the Red Sea's eastern arm

places.name: Mount Nebo
places.note: Moses sees the land he will not enter

places.name: Jericho
places.note: the Jordan crossing, the journey's end

routes.name: “Way of the Philistines”, the short road God did not take them on (Exodus 13:17)

facts: Egypt to Canaan is about 250 miles by the coast road, two weeks of walking. Israel took forty years, and the map shows why the story is about trust, not distance.

God deliberately routed them away from the short coastal road, “for God said, ‘Lest the people change their minds when they see war’” (Exodus 13:17). The grey dashed line is the road they did not take.

Where is Mount Sinai? The traditional answer since at least the 300s AD is Jebel Musa, “the mountain of Moses”, in the south of the Sinai peninsula, where St. Catherine's Monastery still stands. Some scholars argue for other peaks, which is why this map marks it as traditional.

maps.title: Paul's Missionary Journeys
maps.subtitle: Three journeys and a voyage to Rome, from the book of Acts
maps.intro: Every color is one journey. Paul starts at Antioch, works further west each time, and finishes the book of Acts a prisoner in Rome, preaching the whole way.

places.name: Antioch
places.note: home base, every journey starts here

places.name: Salamis
places.note: first stop of the first journey

places.name: Lystra
places.note: stoned and left for dead; Timothy's hometown

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: three years here; the riot of the silversmiths

places.name: Philippi
places.note: Lydia; the jailer; the midnight songs

places.name: Corinth
places.note: a year and a half; two letters later

places.name: Fair Havens
places.note: the harbor they should have stayed in (Acts 27)

places.name: Rome
places.note: the journey's end, “and so we came to Rome”

routes.name: First journey (Acts 13–14), and back the same way

facts: Add the journeys up and Paul covered roughly 10,000 miles, most of it on foot or in small wooden ships, with no maps anywhere near as good as this one.

Each journey pushes further west: the first reaches Cyprus and Galatia, the second crosses into Europe at Philippi, the third is anchored by three years in Ephesus, and the last voyage lands him in Rome itself.
Half the New Testament letters are addressed to cities on this map, find Ephesus, Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth and Rome, and you are looking at the address list of Paul's epistles.

maps.title: The Twelve Tribes of Israel
maps.subtitle: How the Promised Land was divided (Joshua 13–19)
maps.intro: After the conquest, Joshua divided the land among the tribes by lot. The tinted areas are approximate, the Bible describes the borders town by town, and nobody can draw them exactly.
maps.disclaimer: Tribal areas are shown as soft regions, not hard borders, on purpose: Joshua 13–19 lists boundary towns, many of which can no longer be located, so every tribal map is an approximation. The positions here follow the standard reconstructions.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: on the line between Judah and Benjamin

places.name: Shiloh
places.note: where the land was divided by lot (Joshua 18)

places.name: Dan (the city)
places.note: the tribe of Dan moved here later (Judges 18)

facts: Count the areas and you get thirteen, not twelve, because Joseph's inheritance was doubled through his sons Ephraim and Manasseh, and Levi received no land at all. The priests' tribe got 48 towns scattered through everyone else's territory instead (Joshua 21).
Manasseh appears twice: half the tribe settled east of the Jordan with Reuben and Gad before the conquest (Numbers 32), and half took land in the west.

The tribe of Dan was first given the small coastal area near the Philistines, and later gave up and marched to the far north to capture the city they renamed Dan (Judges 18). That is why the city at the land's northern tip carries a southern tribe's name.

maps.title: The Land of Canaan
maps.subtitle: The Promised Land as Joshua found it
maps.intro: The land God promised Abraham, as it looked when Israel finally arrived: walled Canaanite cities, seven nations, and the Jordan to cross first.

places.name: Jericho
places.note: the first city, walls and all (Joshua 6)

places.name: Gibeon
places.note: the clever treaty; the day the sun stood still

places.name: Jerusalem (Jebus)
places.note: still a Jebusite city for 400 more years

facts: God lists the seven nations of Canaan in Deuteronomy 7:1: “Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, seven nations greater and mightier than you.” The map shows where the main ones lived.

The spies carried one cluster of grapes on a pole between two men (Numbers 13:23): it came from the valley near Hebron. Forty years later, Caleb, one of those two faithful spies, asked for that exact hill country as his inheritance.
Jericho sits by the Jordan crossing, which is why it had to be first: it guarded the doorway into the whole land.

timeline.note: The Bible gives no dates for Genesis 1–11, and this chart doesn't invent any.
The exodus is traditionally dated c. 1446 BC; many scholars argue for c. 1270 BC.
